collins.hedgehog: Stop trying to be the top research-driven pharmaceutical company, a race Abbott could not win against Merck. Instead, become best in the world at a portfolio of products that make health care cost-effective: hospital nutritionals, diagnostics, and hospital supplies and products. Collins gives the economic denominator as profit per employee.
hedgehog_key_points: hospital nutritionals, diagnostics and hospital products rather than blockbuster drug discovery
accept it cannot be the best pharmaceutical (Merck-style) company
collins.stop_doing: Stop chasing the goal of being a leading blockbuster-drug company and stop spreading capital into unrelated consumer diversification. Concentrate resources on cost-effective hospital and diagnostic products. Earlier, the leadership also ended the nepotism that had weakened management.
stop_doing_key_points: stop competing head-on as a research-blockbuster pharma company
stop drifting into unrelated consumer diversification
end nepotism / rebuild the management team
collins.leader_type: Level 5. Collins credits George Cain (CEO 1958-72) with rebuilding the board and executive team, breaking the nepotism and setting exacting standards, despite a personality that was not charismatic. The transition itself came under his insider successors (Ledder, then Schoellhorn running hospital products).
brutal_facts: the company had fallen behind in research and had no major new drug in sight
the cyclamate ban and the IV-solution recall exposed management weakness
it could not out-research the pharmaceutical leaders
hospitals and payers were moving toward cost control

later_history: Collins reports cumulative returns about 3.98x the market for 1974-1989. Hospital products revenue rose 139% from 1974 to 1979. Sales nearly tripled in the 1980s under Schoellhorn, with diagnostics growing (including the first AIDS blood test in 1985). Schoellhorn was ousted in 1989. Abbott paid a $100M FDA-related fine in 1999 over diagnostic-kit quality. It stayed independent and large, agreed in 2000 to buy Knoll from BASF for $6.9B, and split off its research pharma business as AbbVie in 2013. No collapse.
notes: Track A matched pair with A04 (Upjohn). The dossier is dated early 1974. Cain died in 1972, so the dossier's CEO is his successor Ledder. Collins's Level 5 attribution is mainly to Cain. Collins's exact economic denominator wording is paraphrased from summaries (LitCharts, Compound Learning) and from memory of Ch. 5, not checked against the book text.
